title: ICYM$^2$I: The illusion of multimodal informativeness under missingness
claim: Naive training and evaluation on curated data gives biased modality-value estimates; correcting with inverse probability weighting recovers reliable target-distribution estimates.
layout: 2 horizontal rows, left-to-right flow, blue current practice versus orange proposed
description: A wide, two-row flow diagram that reads left to right. At the far left, a rounded box shows the collected data Ω as a grid of document and image icons with dotted empty cells for missing modalities. A curation arrow leads to the source dataset Ω_source, which has more missing cells. The blue top row is current practice: training on P(Y|text), P(Y|image) and P(Y|text,image), then evaluation. It ends in the claim that text < image < both, labeled as biased estimates. The orange bottom row is the proposed method: IPW-corrected training and evaluation, which gives corrected estimates with a different ordering, text > image > both. Both rows end at the target data Ω_target box. Blue and orange outcome boxes at the right read 'Suboptimal data collection and modeling decisions' and 'Reliable performance and informativeness estimates'. The color contrast draws the eye first.
caption: Overview of the proposed framework. Curation often discards missing data, resulting in a discrepancy between the collected $\Omega$ and source datasets $\Omega_{source}$ used for training. Current practice is denoted in blue: na\"ive training and evaluating on $\Omega_{source}$ leads to biased estimates of performance and informativeness on target data. The orange path illustrates the proposed \methodname: a double inverse probability weighting (IPW) mechanism that yields accurate performance and informativeness estimates under the target distribution.
abstract: Multimodal learning is of continued interest in artificial intelligence-based applications, motivated by the potential information gain from combining different data modalities. However, modalities observed in the source environment may differ from the modalities observed in the target environment due to multiple factors, including cost, hardware failure, or the perceived \textit{informativeness} of a given modality. This change in missingness patterns between the source and target environment has not been carefully studied. Na{Ã¯}ve estimation of the information gain associated with including an additional modality without accounting for missingness may result in improper estimates of that modality's value in the target environment. We formalize the problem of missingness, demonstrate its ubiquity, and show that the subsequent distribution shift induces bias when the missingness process is not explicitly accounted for. To address this issue, we introduce ICYM2I (In Case You Multimodal Missed It), a framework for the evaluation of predictive performance and information gain under missingness through inverse probability weighting-based correction. We demonstrate the importance of the proposed adjustment to estimate information gain under missingness on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world datasets.
